newsitem.title: USA: Clean up begins in tornado-ravaged Texas town.
newsitem.headline: Clean up begins in tornado-ravaged Texas town.

text.p: Survivors began picking up what few pieces of their lives were left behind on Thursday after a tornado ripped through this central Texas town two days ago, killing 27 people and leaving dozens more homeless.

Residents of a subdivision leveled by the twister found muddied clothing or battered pictures in the debris, but many were left with little more than a deepened sense of shock after finding nothing had been spared by the storm.
"It's total devastation, more than can be described," Darlene Applegate told reporters as she stood clutching her 6-year-old granddaughter outside a police checkpoint.

Rescuers combing through the rubble of the Double Creek Estates subdivision since Tuesday found the bodies of 27 victims, and police on Thursday located a survivor who was reported missing and believed dead, a police spokeswoman said.

"We have 27 bodies and 27 names of people unaccounted for. We expect that those will match. As far as we know, this is our best estimate" of the final final death toll, Texas Department of Public Safety spokeswoman Laureen Chernow said.
Some survivors saw little need to return to a neighbourhood where more than 50 houses and mobile homes were ripped from their foundations and blown apart in the deadly storm.

"Today there was the smell of death over the whole area. It was no use to go back down there because there was nothing left to find," Charlie Boren said. "I'm just going to sign the release so the county can bulldoze it."

Officials have begun the grim process of notifying families that their missing relatives were among the people killed by the storm in Jarrell, a small town of some 600 people about 40 miles (64 km) north of Austin.

"I know what I went through and I know what they went through. I just hope it happened fast for them," said Virginia Davidson, who survived the storm by huddling in a bathtub and covering herself with a blanket.

As the twister swept through the neighbourhood with winds approaching 300 miles (480 km) per hour, Davidson and the tub she was in were tossed 100 feet (30 metres) from her demolished house. She survived with bruises and cuts.

Some residents had grown restless to return to their homes, many of which were swept away as a line of storms spawned at least six tornadoes that also killed two people and collapsed the roof of a grocery store near Austin.
Police kept up a tight perimeter around the Jarrell neighbourhood, which is dotted with cement foundations where homes once stood, as they searched for victims.
James Taylor, a 38-year-old electrician, said he got a black eye when he was beaten with a police flashlight and arrested on Tuesday while trying to get to his home.
"I was going to go back to see about my neighbourhood, to see about my property, to see about my house," he said. "They started whipping me."
Police said it may take weeks to identify all of the mangled bodies of the tornado victims. Four people identified so far included a 5-year-old boy, a 44-year-old woman and two school-age brothers.

Max Johnson, pastor of the First Baptist Church, said the town's grieving process could now finally begin. "It has been kind of frustrating because of all the unknowns ... it's like a thorn in your foot you need to pull out," he said.
